This message is shown only once. Please take a few minutes to read it:

Thank you for choosing KookYar. This app is the result of more than a year of research in Persian traditional music and audio processing. KookYar helps you tune Persian and Western instruments easily, especially for beginners. The app is still evolving — your feedback helps us improve it. Use Send feedback in the main menu. We hope KookYar brings more people to music.

To tune your instrument, select a string and use the tuner gauge. If the needle is left of center, tighten (clockwise) until it turns green on the center line. If it is right of center, loosen (counter-clockwise). Start from the first string and tune in order.
Select a dastgah tuning, then tune each bridge using the needle gauge.

Below are the factors that affect the sound of a santur: 
 1- Mallet weight: 
 The weight of the mezrabs (mallets) usually affects the volume of the sound. Light mezrabs are mostly thinner and also have a small, thin head, which means that when they strike the string they lack the necessary or sufficient force, so the resulting sound has little volume. With heavy mezrabs it is the other way round.
 2- How closely the right and left mallets match in weight, size, thickness and material: 
As a rule and by standard, the pair of mezrabs a player holds is assumed to be identical in every respect; otherwise there will be a difference both in the volume of the right and left mallets and in the colour and amount of ring in the sound. 
 3- The mallet's centre of gravity: 
The centre of gravity of a mezrab is usually located roughly in its first quarter. Naturally, depending on how far forward or back the centre of gravity is, the way the mallet plays changes slightly, which ultimately causes a small change in the sound produced. 
 4- The proportions of the ring, shaft and head of the mallet: 
 Clearly, correct and precise proportions between these elements are what make an ideal, standard mezrab, in which case its centre of gravity will also sit in the right place. Not observing these proportions precisely affects the way the mallet plays and ultimately makes a difference in the instrument's sound. 
 5- Mallet material: 
For players who play without felt, the material of their mezrab determines its weight and the volume of the sound, and whether the sound is soft, dry or ringing. 
 6- Felt material and thickness, and how it is glued: 
Naturally, the thicker the felt, the more muffled the sound, and the thinner the felt, the more open the sound will be. Different felts made of different materials mostly have different tone colours, and which tone colour a player prefers, and which felt of what thickness to use, is a matter of experience and taste. If a solid (dry) adhesive is used to attach the felt, the resulting sound will be just as expected; but if a liquid glue is used, so that the glue soaks through to both sides of the felt, the sound will have a little ring to it. 
 7- How the mallets are held: 
As we know, the way of holding the mezrab has changed somewhat from the old days to the present (depending on the mallet model). The shape of your mezrab and how you hold it define your way of playing and, to some extent, your command of the instrument, and together these make a certain difference in the resulting sound. 
 8- Striking technique: 
 Basically there are several ways of playing the mezrab: with the fingers only – with the wrist only – with the forearm only – with the fingers and wrist together – with the wrist and forearm together – and with all three, i.e. fingers, wrist and forearm. It should be added, of course, that in every style the stroke is the resultant of forces coming from the spine, shoulders, forearm, wrist and fingers. The sound produced by your santur will differ in proportion to how you strike. 
 9- Where the mallets land: 
When you strike closer to the kharaks (bridges), the sound is drier and harsher; the farther from the bridges you strike, the softer and gentler the tones will be. 
 10- How the santur is placed: 
 Your instrument's sound will change according to how much of the santur's bottom board is free of contact with anything while playing, or, where it does touch something, what material it rests on (wood, metal, fabric, etc.).

The factors above may account for anywhere from half a percent to perhaps seventy percent of the sound produced by an instrument (in its volume, quality and tone colour). In my opinion, however, more important than all of these is what kind of sound the musical ear of the player, given their own style and taste, wants to draw from the instrument, and how; naturally, all of the factors above are subordinate to this power of discernment and to the player's taste. 

Apart from the factors already mentioned, other things can also make a difference to an instrument's sound, for example its tuning: whether it is tuned exactly to the tuning fork, or higher or lower, which in turn determines the tension of the strings (tight or slack) and so defines how soft or harsh the sound is. 

Finally, it should be added that other things such as how warm or cold the air is, the humidity, the space in which the instrument is played (outdoors, indoors, a fully enclosed room) and many other factors can contribute to the variety of sound produced by a santur.
 Source: Saman Zarrabi – Harmonic discussion site

Broadly speaking, the whole set of activities a student goes through to acquire this skill – that is, “recognising a good instrument” – takes at least seven to ten years, depending on talent and progress, and its main prerequisites are briefly outlined below: 
 1- Listening seriously to music (santur music) until one reaches a good level of musical understanding and appreciation of the beautiful sound of this instrument. 
 2- Enough practice and progress to be able to perform (at least semi-) professional santur pieces, so that one can use them as a yardstick for identifying a good instrument. 
 3- Some knowledge of how the instrument is made, so that one can also evaluate it in terms of appearance. 
 4- Playing and practising on all kinds of santurs (very good ones and very bad ones) 

Given these conditions, a student who does not yet have enough experience and knowledge of a high-quality instrument has several options: 
 1- Buy an expensive instrument blindly because the seller said it is a good one, until the day they become an expert themselves. 
 2- Trust one of the makers or sellers to give them, hopefully, a good-quality instrument at a reasonable price. 
 3- Or rely on their teacher and buy an instrument on the teacher's direct advice. Provided there is no “collusion” (a backroom deal between teacher and seller) involved, this third option seems the most sensible and logical (unfortunately, many students have been hurt by exactly this kind of “collusion”). 
 4- Another option exists, but it is very difficult, time-consuming and confusing: the student gathers details of several good instruments from several makers or sellers, takes each of those instruments to a few respected masters, gets their approval of the instruments, or of one of them as the best, and only then buys. 

The advice that I, as the least experienced member of the music community, give to students is that students of the santur, and indeed of other instruments, should not go looking for a top-grade instrument at all, except in two cases: 
 One is that they have themselves acquired, to a reasonable degree, the ability to recognise a good instrument, so that they are not entirely dependent on others and can also offer an opinion of their own about the instrument; the other is that they place complete trust in one, and only one, teacher whom they rely on, and buy their good instrument on that teacher's direct advice – knowing that this good instrument they have bought may in the future be criticised by makers, by various masters and even by themselves, so that if this prediction comes true they will have no complaint later against their teacher or the person they trusted. 
 In general, every instrument can be evaluated from three points of view: 
 1- Appearance 
 2- Quality of the materials used 
 3- Quality of the sound produced (the result of the engineering of the instrument's construction) 
 
 Clearly, examining an instrument and rating it as good, average or bad depends on examining the factors above. It is worth noting that these three factors are not “completely” independent of one another and cannot be evaluated entirely separately; for example, a good santur is certainly made of materials of average-to-high quality, and its appearance has certainly been attended to in order to achieve good sound quality. 
 Appearance: 
 The factors that can be named here are, in list form: 
 1- Colour of the instrument 
 2- Proportions of the dimensions 
 3- Decoration 
 4- Shape and colour of the bridges 
 5- Shape of the santur's rosettes (sound holes) 
 6- How the strings are hooked 
 7- How the strings are wound around the tuning pins 
 8- Cleanness of workmanship 
 9- Soundness of the top board, bottom board and frames 
 1- Colour of the instrument: 
 Bright or subdued colours make no difference and are a matter of the buyer's taste, provided that the colour of the wood has not been botched during the making and finishing of the instrument in a way that spoils its sound. Of course, a colour that matches the colour of the bridges gives the instrument a nicer look. 
 2- Proportions of the dimensions: 
 Since, as mentioned in previous issues, there is no standard for building a santur, and it is not precisely known which dimensions (length, width, height and the thickness of each part, such as the top board) should be specified in the building instructions to produce a better sound, measuring the length, width and thickness down to the centimetre will not mean much. Santur makers have on the whole arrived at good proportions, but the golden dimensions and proportions for achieving the desired quality are still not precisely known. Still, if at a quick glance there is an acceptable proportion between the instrument's dimensions, that is enough as far as appearance is concerned. 
 3- Inlay work: 
 If the khatam (marquetry inlay) work, engravings and decorations are done in a way that has not damaged the wood, they generally do not hinder the sound; but decorated instruments are not usually favoured by players, unless they want to use the instrument for display in a showcase. 
 4- Bridges: 
 The shape of the bridges has no effect on the sound at all, but their height does. Of course, bridge height has by and large been standardised, and there does not seem to be any problem in this regard. That leaves the colour of the bridges, which again depends on personal taste. 
 5- The santur's rosettes: 
 In general, the shape of a santur's rosette does not affect its sound, though its size has a very small effect on the instrument's volume. The position of the rosette on the santur, however, is important and can affect sound quality; in most santurs this, too, has found its proper place thanks to the makers' knowledge, and you will rarely find a santur whose rosettes are not in a suitable position. 
 6- String hooks: 
 The way the strings are hooked and the shape of the hooks do not affect the instrument's sound; the hook simply needs to be complete and sound so that it does not cause the string to break. 
 7- Winding the strings around the tuning pins: 
 Like the hooking, the winding of the strings has no effect on the instrument's sound; it is simply better if it is done neatly and cleanly and looks good. The only requirement is that the strings be wound onto the pins correctly so that they do not break during tuning. 
 8- Cleanness of workmanship: 
 The top and bottom boards should fit tightly against the top, bottom, right and left frames, with no protrusions on any side. There should be no visible traces of glue. The tuning pins and hitch pins should be in neat, orderly rows, without any damage to the wood. 
 9- Soundness of the wood: 
 There should be no cracks, breaks, swelling or dents, especially in the top and bottom boards; if these have a problem, the instrument will usually never sound good again. But if there is a minor problem in the side frames or the top and bottom frames, it can be repaired, and one can expect the instrument's sound not to be spoiled after the repair. 
 Quality of the materials used
 There is not a great variety of materials used to build a santur: 
 The body is most often made of walnut, sometimes of azad (Caucasian elm) and sometimes of other forest woods. The tuning pins, hitch pins and the rods on top of the bridges are metal (iron). 

The white strings are steel, and the yellow strings are brass or copper. 

Now, these same materials can be relatively poor, average or good. There is not much variety in the quality of the white strings: they are all steel and their quality is “almost” the same. Yellow brass strings are better than copper ones (brass strings are yellow and copper strings are reddish). It is best that they be of good quality, free of scratches and rust. 
 The metal used for the tuning pins and hitch pins also does not vary much in quality, and whether it is good or bad has no effect on the sound of the instrument. But the quality of the metal used for the rods on the bridges and on the sheytanaks (the nut rails along the sides) matters more, because these are in direct contact with the strings, so it is best that they be of good quality, free of scratches and rust. 

The most important part, of exceptional importance in building a santur, is its wood. According to makers' many years of experience, the best wood for the job is walnut. But the mere fact that a santur is made of walnut should not lead students to the mistaken assumption that there is nothing more to be said; rather, using walnut, subject to certain conditions, can do a great deal to improve the quality of a santur's sound. Among the conditions I can mention, which are also within a student's practical knowledge, are: 
 First, the quality of the wood itself and how it is worked and finished. 
 Second, which part of the walnut tree has been used for which part of the santur. 
 Since the top and bottom boards are the most important parts of a santur, it matters which part of the wood has been used to make and finish them. The side, top and bottom frames are less important, and naturally care in choosing which part of the wood to use for them, and how to process it, matters less. 
 The third important point is to use wood that has dried completely – naturally, over time. Wood cut from a tree for use usually needs many, many years to dry fully and be ready for use. One of the problems we face today is mass production: naturally, with makers building instruments at high speed, the wood is not given the time it needs to dry, so they use wood whose fibres still hold more or less moisture. It would not be surprising if such instruments, in the not-too-distant future, developed problems such as a bulging top board or a swollen bottom board, especially if the player has to perform in varying climatic conditions. 

Of course, today, thanks to the knowledge makers have gained of different woods and how to work and finish them, and also through new techniques some makers use to dry wood, this problem has been solved to an acceptable degree; but such wood still cannot be compared with sound walnut that has been drying for about twenty years since it was cut. 

Fourth, since a player usually needs to perform with their instrument in different places, under different conditions and in various seasons, an important point in construction is using good wood and working and finishing it properly, so that the body of the instrument becomes resistant to natural hardships: heat, cold, humidity, transport, knocks and falls (for example off a table, or inside the case while being carried). 

There are exceptions too. In rare cases one sees a santur in which good wood has been used and, even though the engineering and the materials used are not even of average grade, the sound of the instrument is still pleasing and standard – sometimes on the level of a first-grade instrument and sometimes of a second-grade one. 

In fact, these explanations make it clear that “the engineering of the instrument's construction”, with good wood as its prerequisite, comes first in importance, ahead of the instrument's appearance and the materials used. 
 Quality of the resulting sound: 
 In general, to this day it is very hard to judge which of the very good instruments are truly first-grade. Until “instrument making” and “organology” are regarded and practised as professional disciplines, a consensus is reached, and instrument quality is standardised at different levels, the situation will remain as it is. So, for example, an instrument that one master prices at one million tomans may well be considered average by another master, who would not price it above four hundred thousand tomans. Until this chaotic market is put in order, personal taste will always act as the most influential ingredient, with the result that we keep drifting further from the question of standards, since the range of people's tastes is very wide and depends on many different factors. 

A trained ear easily tells a grade 1, 2 or 3 santur apart, and when a professional player sets out to buy a grade 1 instrument, taking into account the technical aspects of its construction and its sound quality, they will certainly choose the instrument that is closest to their own taste (since for now there is no other option). 

Of course, this method of selection – that is, the role of taste in professional players' choice of instrument – is customary all over the world; but players' taste in no way fills the gap left by the absence of a standard. “Having standards for instruments” and “players' taste” are two completely separate matters. Therefore “taste” has no place in a technical discussion, and dwelling on it is fruitless. 

A brief definition of a first-grade instrument: an instrument whose appearance is acceptable in every technical and constructional respect and which has a very pleasing sound quality – according, of course, to the current definition of the existing standard, and leaving aside questions of style and taste. (The current standard means the taste of the masters in choosing instruments for performance, most of whose recordings are available.) 

Generally, the masters hold more or less differing, taste-based opinions about what makes a good, first-grade instrument: 
 1- A good santur is one that responds well when playing the radif (the traditional repertoire of Persian classical music), whose sound is closer to that of the old masters' instruments, and whose authentic sound is preserved. 
 2- On a first-grade instrument one should be able to perform first-rate technical pieces well; the instrument should have a modern character and be in harmony and keeping with today's pieces and today's atmosphere, rather than with the sound and music of the old masters. 
 3- Some masters have in mind a particular model from a certain master (old or contemporary), and in their view the closer an instrument is to that model, the better it is. 
 4- Others believe that no instrument can be considered first-grade in absolute terms; rather, in each style there is a first-grade instrument which, compared with another style, might count as second- or third-grade. 

In any case, the criteria by which the sound quality of a santur can be assessed are, in brief: 
 -Correct and logical spacing of the three positions (registers): when notes are played in succession from the lowest to the highest, they should be completely continuous; for example, the sound of the second bridge of the white strings (the note F) should follow right after the eighth bridge of the yellow strings (the note E), and the change of position should not be noticeable. 
 -Consistency of tone colour between the white strings, the yellow strings and the strings behind the bridges, so that when, during a piece, you play on the white strings and then immediately on the yellow strings, you do not get the feeling that the piece is being played on two santurs; rather, the white and yellow strings should sound as a single voice from one santur. 
 -How long the resonance of a note lasts, under soft, normal and strong strokes. The idea that the longer a note rings after it is struck the better is not correct; the vibration of the string after the stroke has a limit (around 3 to 6 seconds), because otherwise the sounds blend into one another and the instrument loses its musicality. 
 -A suitable overall volume. Contrary to what some beginners think, a loud instrument is never a sign of good sound quality. The volume of the instrument should be moderate; how much counts as moderate comes down to the player's experience and knowledge of the instrument's sound. -A sound that is not monotonous, so that it does not tire the ears of the player and the listener. Naturally, a student must have listened to different santurs for hours to know which sound is monotonous and which is not; naturally, gaining experience of this takes several years of work. 
 -Clarity and preserved sound quality when playing very soft and very strong strokes. On some instruments, a very soft stroke cannot be heard at all, and a very strong stroke produces nothing but a loud blare of a note (so-called noise). 
 -The sound should be neither nasal nor too loose (neither choked, nor unbridled and wild). 
 -A certain amount of hollow, woody resonance and ring (recognising these last two depends on the player's familiarity with the sound of the instrument). 

(There are certainly other criteria too; those above are simply what occurred to the author within the scope of this article.) Another important point is that, knowing all of the above, an expert player usually makes the final choice of a good instrument by picking, with the help of these factors, from among several fairly good instruments; the next stage is that the player, depending on their listening skill, plays the selected instruments for a few days, a week or a month, so as to finally choose the instrument they like in every respect. It is unreasonable to expect a professional player to confirm on the spot that an instrument is first-grade on seeing it for the first time or after playing one or two pieces on it. 

Other ways of examining the quality and character of an instrument's sound include playing it in various settings, such as: outdoors – in a studio – in hot and cold weather – in humid weather – with felted and unfelted mezrabs (mallets) – in small and large halls (with a microphone). Of course, these are mentioned so that santur students are aware of such matters; it may not always be possible to put an instrument through all of the conditions above and test it. 

Another way of examining it is to play technical santur pieces with good mezrabs without felt, because experience shows that on very good santurs, playing with felted or unfelted mezrabs does not make much difference in either the volume or the quality of the sound, and both sounds are good and acceptable. 

All in all, it seems that an instrument should strike a balance: it should more or less recall the sound of the old masters' instruments without straying too far from the traditional sound of the santur, and at the same time one should be able to perform today's technical pieces on it (in general) – unless someone has clearly chosen their own playing strategy, which is a separate matter. It seems that a santur with such balance and proportion would be a step towards establishing standards. 
 Source: Saman Zarrabi – Harmonic discussion site

Below are some points that, taken together, make an instrument sound better:

The instrument settling in (or, as it is called, being “broken in”): 
 It is said that the more an instrument is played, the better and more mature its sound becomes. This is true, but not for every instrument of every quality; it applies only to good and very good instruments. To make this clear, let me give an example. 

If you know a little about carpets, you know that a fine, good-quality carpet, after many long years of being spread underfoot – of being “walked on”, as they say – gradually grows in artistic and material value. You may even have come across carpets that have been walked on for 30, 40 or 50 years being hung on the wall and displayed before everyone as valuable works of art, and how proud people are of them! 

By comparison, you have surely seen what becomes of a poor, low-quality carpet. After only a few years of being spread underfoot, its warp and weft gradually show through and come apart, and little by little its condition reaches the point where keeping it is not a source of pride but an embarrassment. The example above is exactly the story of the instrument. 

Every good instrument has the capacity to get better (in terms of sound). If yours is a good, first-grade instrument, you can hope that by playing it a lot it will become better, more mature and more seasoned year by year; and in principle the word and the concept of “breaking in” only make sense for such instruments. 

A bad instrument, however, is exactly like a low-quality carpet: after a certain period of playing, at the point when the instrument is expected to have broken in and to be approaching its mature, true sound, the poor quality of its sound is so obvious that even beginner students notice it clearly. So the time you would expect such an instrument to be broken in is the time when you should throw it away. In other words, instruments of this kind are bearable only while they are brand new. 
 Protecting the instrument:
 Do not let it be knocked – keep it out of the direct path of cold and hot air – keep it away from humid air – do not let it get wet or rained on – keep it out of direct sunlight – use a humidity absorber (desiccant) inside the instrument case. 

It is true that caring for the instrument is necessary, on top of your instrument being a good one. On the other hand, too much care makes the instrument temperamental and fussy, and it will trouble the player (the instrument becomes “pampered”, as they say). 

If an instrument has never experienced heat, cold or humidity, then when the player has to play in unusual, non-standard conditions, it will neither tune well nor hold its tuning well, nor will its true sound be heard. 

Even when a santur has stayed in one particular spot at home for years without being moved, if you move it somewhere else (for example from a bedroom to the living room), the change in its sound and the loss of its stability become quite obvious. 

If you have a good instrument, it is better to play it in different places (not every day, but once a week or once every two weeks), and occasionally, not too often, to play it somewhere a little warmer or colder than its usual place, or for example somewhere a little humid (though not for very long). 

Doing this, first, helps the instrument break in and learn to adapt to different environmental conditions (according to the experience of most experts), so that its tone does not change and it does not easily go out of tune, and a good player can use their instrument with peace of mind anywhere and at any event. 
 Sufficient and correct practice:
 Since the sound of a good instrument develops the more it is played, it depends on its player's practice. But can we expect the instrument's sound to improve with any kind of practice, or with any method of somehow hitting or pounding the strings with the mezrab (mallet), or not? 

Experience has made it clear that scattered, aimless playing and playing disjointed fragments of pieces does not help the instrument's sound take shape. Rather, pieces should be played, as far as possible, completely, cleanly and correctly, so that the instrument gradually grows along with correct pieces and a skilled player with a fine touch. 
 Always keeping the instrument in tune: 
 In terms of the wood: when you play an instrument that is in tune only some of the time and out of tune most of the time, the resonance of the discordant sounds produced after each stroke gradually creates irregular highs and lows in the top board's wood (this has long been established in laboratory studies, and I do not intend to go into it in detail, since it is not my field either). Now suppose a student has played this way for five years and then, having learned to tune to an acceptable standard, wants to tune their santur fully and correctly: when they adjust the strings, the vibration and resonance created by the tuned strings, and the effect they have on the wood, are completely harmonious, and they are at odds with the earlier discordant highs and lows formed in the wood. 

So even though the instrument is perfectly in tune, the pleasing sound expected from that santur is not heard. In fact, wood behaves according to the sounds that strike it, keeps that shape and form, and a particular response (in terms of sound) becomes defined for it, and it always responds in that way. So when your instrument is always in tune, it passes harmonious vibrations to the wood; the wood becomes “tamed”, as they say, and learns the right sound. 

The top board of a santur is under two pressures. The first is when the instrument is fully in tune, in which case its strings are fully stretched and exert sufficient pressure on the top board. The second, lesser or greater, depends on how skilfully a player delivers continuous mezrab strokes to the strings with speed and power. Taking these two factors together, the total pressure the top board of a santur bears is roughly more than two hundred kilograms. 

As a result, the expected (standard) pressure on the top board presses on the internal braces of the santur and on the top, bottom and side frames, and over time these become as tight as they can be, until there is no room left for them to tighten further. At that point there is no more room for the strings to stretch or for the different parts of the wood to settle together. 

Now imagine a santur that is not in tune: its strings are not tight enough and do not exert enough pressure on the board, and no matter how hard the player strikes the instrument (which is not the right thing to do anyway), they cannot create that kind of pressure. In that case the various parts of the instrument's body will not settle together any time soon, and naturally the instrument takes longer to settle in. 

In terms of the strings: part of an instrument settling in has to do with the strings settling in (stretching enough that there is no room left for them to stretch further). This, too, can be achieved by trying to keep the instrument in tune as much as possible. So it is best for a player to work for a while with an instrument that is fully in tune, until the strings lose their brand-new state and contribute to the instrument's pleasing sound. 

In terms of the tuning pins: when your instrument has always been kept in tune, tuning it becomes easy, because the pins have always been in the right position and stay fixed in place. But on an instrument that has never been properly in tune, the pins have never been in the right position and end up somewhere different each time; so when we want to tune such an instrument correctly and fully, neither the pins, nor the strings, nor the wood of the instrument (in terms of sound) cooperate. 
 Source: Saman Zarrabi – Harmonic discussion site
